extracted.intended_audience: newspaper reporters (church beat reporters / city reporters learning feature and interview technique)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reporters on planning, writing, and displaying church/sermon stories and on interviewing sources effectively for newspaper coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of sermon stories (Blocks i–6)
rubrics_metrics.description: The structure: Block i: Lead (Sermon or other matter); Block 2: Secondary lead (Other matter or sermon); Block 3: Catch-all; Block 4: Amplification of Block i; Block 5: Amplification of Block 2; Block 6: Lists of names, musical programs, or other details mentioned but not detailed in Blocks 4 and 5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this block structure to organize sermon digests so leads and amplifications are clear; Block 6 holds peripheral details not expanded in Blocks 4 and 5.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrangement option — single long account
rubrics_metrics.description: Run all sermons into one long account, with a combination lead or a lead and secondary lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Saves copy-desk work (only one headline) but drawbacks include most sermons being submerged and an overly long story that may be unsuitable for make-up. Example lead and follow-on lines provided in text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrangement option — separate story per sermon
rubrics_metrics.description: Make a separate story of each sermon, thereby giving each minister a headline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If space permits, lead the 'sermon page' with a roundup or superdigest of the seven or eight best sermons; this treats each sermon distinctly and avoids burying most ministers in one long piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead style: name-led vs statement-led openings
rubrics_metrics.description: Some papers start with a minister's name; others start with a statement (quote) from the sermon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement-led openings are livelier but make transitions between sermons less clear. Use the style that best balances liveliness and clarity of transition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special Sundays — mood stories and descriptive coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain Sundays (near Christmas, Easter, Palm Sunday) permit 'mood' stories that are longer and much more descriptive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fill stories with color, reproduce feelings as well as thoughts, but remember 'overwriting is fatal.' These stories will be eagerly read because churchgoers wish to 'live over again' the service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use temporal links judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: Sundays linked to temporal observance (e.g., July 4, February 22) permit powerful, 'triphammer' writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that temporal links produce rational/mental emphasis rather than the emotional tone of a religious observance like Easter; match tone accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat publicity-hunting ministers cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify that a spectacular or outspoken minister 'really resounds' and is not merely 'word-juggling' or seeking page-one notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume every flamboyant statement deserves large space; be ready to reduce prominence if the preacher's prominence is manufactured or later wanes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance prominence among ministers
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid unduly privileging one publicity-seeking minister at the expense of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Politically boost other ministers (e.g., give them four inches even if it means trimming the celebrity preacher) and be quick to cut down the acrobat's prominence when sermons degenerate into mere vocabulary twists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle anti-newspaper remarks proportionally
rubrics_metrics.description: When a preacher attacks newspapers, determine whether the attack is integral to the sermon or simply 'shotgunning for page i.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If integral, lead with it; if merely thrown in for publicity, 'give it what it deserves and no more.' Do not overplay diatribes against the press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'bulletin-board' Saturday pages — invigorate the page
rubrics_metrics.description: Fifteen or twenty advance notices of sermon subjects and music in bland form make doleful reading; a page that is only a bulletin board is too feeble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two safe practices: (1) have each week a 'lead story' about a particular church activity; (2) save for Saturday safe midweek stories gathered earlier that won't be used by competing papers; consider treating some stories as held by treaty with rivals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pictures and size them by story importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Pictures often decorate the church page; ministers with appropriate topics may be good for one-column pictures; new officers may merit two- or three-column photos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign photo size in proportion to the news value of the event (sermon topic suitability or organizational news).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain predictable page length and coordinate with make-up editor
rubrics_metrics.description: The Saturday page must run about the same amount of type from one week to another so the make-up editor can plan placement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a marked departure is unavoidable, notify the make-up editor early (the day before if possible); this cooperation helps the make-up editor schedule pages without wrecking others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat midweek 'Dorcas' and small society stories as valuable — give them feature treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Dorcas Guild stories and similar midweek notices may be written flatly; they are nevertheless 'distinctly worth while.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ponder such stories, equip them with a first-line feature, use your best writing to make them powerful (but not freakish), and write them so they suggest a good headline to reduce copy-desk resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage limited staffing by prioritizing coverage and using second-hand sources
rubrics_metrics.description: When city editor gives the church reporter limited time, the reporter must know which events require his presence and which can be handled by telephone or volunteers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train press chairmen to supply adequate information; arrange to telephone a responsible officer after meetings to get the essentials; do not neglect tidbits because coverage is fast-moving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use annual meetings as regular firsthand coverage — be consistent in praise
rubrics_metrics.description: Annual church meetings are always covered firsthand and may be gilded with flattering adjectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you praise one church as having a 'most successful year' you must apply similar praise consistently to comparable churches. 'Praise and adjectives must be used always, or never.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Be tolerant: give routine attention to fringe and minority churches
rubrics_metrics.description: Tiny or seemingly primitive sects (e.g., 'Church of the Brothers and Sisters of Jehovah's Covenant') and churches with imposing names deserve routine attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ridiculing or using such congregations as 'comic relief.' Though coverage may be less frequent than larger churches, giving routine notice prevents members feeling discriminated against and recognizes their readership value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate coverage and sources for Negro, Jewish, and Catholic congregations
rubrics_metrics.description: Negro and Jewish churches are often overlooked; Catholic services often receive less space because clergy have been less receptive and multiple Sunday services make full coverage space-consuming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be sincere and persevering; gather some information second-hand until accepted; cultivate contacts even for Catholics (tips on transfers, anniversaries); do not neglect these communities or assume they're opposed to publicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask for good display: secure departmental labeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Persuade the make-up editor to use the 'Religious News' heading whenever there is a half-column or so of type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a news department with high potentiality, persistent digging for news will encourage regular use of the department label and better display of church coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn and respect church terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: The churchmen's language is worth the learning; some clergy prefer 'pastor' and others 'minister.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using preferred titles helps the reporter's friendliness and relations with clergy; it dispels notions that churches are newsworthy only when discredited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interviewing is a core journalistic skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Interviewing ranks high because it is the basis for much news — many stories are obtained, developed, or expanded through interviewing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize interviewing as obtaining information by asking questions; master it to produce stories beyond mere record rewrites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary 1 — find out who he is (research the interviewee)
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn everything possible about the person before the interview: Who is he? What has he done? His likes, dislikes, hobbies, peeves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use newspaper reference files, Who's Who, public library, and acquaintances; advance knowledge helps frame appropriate questions and signals to the interviewee that you understand his subject and lingo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary 2 — write out the questions in advance
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare a written list of questions before the interview rather than relying on ad-libbing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without a plan, the interview may yield little usable material and the reporter is vulnerable to stage fright or taciturn interviewees. Memorized or prepared queries can carry the interview through difficult moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: The reporter is the ringmaster — direct and control the interview
rubrics_metrics.description: The reporter must direct the interview, swinging it away from unproductive discussions toward printable aspects; he cannot rely on random questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think of the interviewer as an architect with a plan; the unplanned reporter will get no more than a two-minute telephone call's worth of information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage different interviewee behaviors (reluctant, mendacious, overtalkative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interviewees may be reluctant, deceitful, overtalkative with little truth, or simply ignorant of what is news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reporter must 'manage people' — coax, dig deep, distinguish genuine from propaganda, and prompt those who don't know what to say; sales and subscription soliciting experience are recommended preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: The vital first minute — introduce yourself and state purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The first sixty seconds often determine success; the good interviewer introduces himself formally as a reporter and states his purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid surprises later ('I didn't realize you wanted to print this'); present the interview as an opportunity for the interviewee to speak as an authority — reduce antagonism and stage fright quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare subject knowledge when interview focuses on a specific topic
rubrics_metrics.description: When an interview centers on a particular subject, the reporter learns as much as possible about that field beforehand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An informed reporter can follow discussions intelligently, avoid frequent interruptions for clarification, and be trusted to get quotations correctly — lack of subject knowledge insults experts and wastes time.

rubrics_metrics.name: When staff/time limited, triage interviews and use substitutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Some interviews must be handled in haste; avoid hasty face-to-face interviews if they will be unproductive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, avoid rushed interviews, assign easier items to telephone or volunteers, and recognize which meetings require the reporter to attend in person.
